A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DECEPTIONDECODED and the same underlying research. Their text, tables, figures, prompts, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added studies in v3.

before.justification: V1 reports original VLM evaluations, human verification, modality and prompting analyses, and an image-generator comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds human realism and intent-alignment studies plus fine-tuning transfer results.

M1.justification: The GPT-4o/FLUX data-generation pipeline and implication-oriented and consistency-oriented inference prompts remain unchanged. V3 adds a limited training adaptation for transfer: full-parameter fine-tuning of two 7B VLMs using image-caption inputs and answer-only binary supervision (Appendix F.5).

E1.justification: MMFakeBench, previously discussed only as related work, becomes an evaluated external dataset in v3. Its general misinformation classification task extends coverage beyond the internally generated intent benchmark. The original 12,000 instances, ten source topics, and three intent-centric tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 3 removes Claude-3.5-Sonnet from creator-desire inference, reducing that comparison from nine models to eight. The main 14-model comparison is retained; the appendices confirm that the revised Qwen and Llama names identify the same models. The new transfer experiment compares pretrained and fine-tuned variants of two existing 7B models.

E3.justification: V3 introduces a transfer protocol using 6,000 training examples, 1,000 per intent category, one epoch, binary label mapping, and evaluation on 1,000 MMFakeBench validation examples comprising 700 fake and 300 real cases. Table 6 reports Macro-F1 and Macro-Acc. New human protocols assess 120 examples per modality for standalone plausibility and 80 misleading examples per modality for pairwise plausibility and intent alignment. Retained experiments keep their settings.

E4.justification: V1's human verification checks misleading versus non-misleading labels. V3 substantially extends validation to standalone and pairwise realism, desired-influence alignment, and execution-plan alignment (Appendices E.2–E.3). It also tests downstream transfer utility. Existing modality, style, authenticity-hint, and image-fidelity analyses remain; Table 9 adds illustrative pairs to the existing style analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions specify one evaluation run at temperature zero and report human agreement through accuracy and Fleiss' kappa. V3 applies the same reporting practice to additional human studies. It introduces no repeated-run estimates, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V3 adds pretrained-to-fine-tuned MMFakeBench macro-F1 results of 44.41 to 52.37 for LLaVA and 27.96 to 58.66 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Table 6). New human findings include text/image standalone plausibility of 98.3%/91.7% and desire alignment of 92.5%/86.3%. Section 5.2 newly reports successful misleading image generation for all 200 cases despite guardrails. Claude-3.5-Sonnet's desire-inference results are removed. Retained detection, modality, hint, and image-generator table values are unchanged.

T1.justification: The news-triplet formulations and desired-influence/execution-plan representation remain unchanged. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs, and v3 adds no mathematical derivation or substantive formal definition.

C1.justification: The central claims about the benchmark, three tasks, and VLM reliance on superficial cues remain. V3's introduction adds the claim that training on DECEPTIONDECODED improves external misinformation detection, extending its claimed utility beyond evaluation. This is a limited expansion of the retained contributions.

C2.justification: V3 interprets the new studies as evidence of realistic, intent-aligned data and broader training utility. Section 5.2 adds a guardrail-bypass risk interpretation, while Appendix B clarifies that the target is unsupported distortion while respecting diverse viewpoints. The limitations concerning open-ended intent evaluation and unmeasured societal influence are retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: Appendix F.5 adds a substantial fine-tuning recipe: prompt masking, answer-span matching, data shuffling, left padding without truncation, learning rate 1e-5, effective batch size 32, bf16 precision, and the Figure 11 prompt. V3 also documents new annotation questions and explicitly specifies majority-vote aggregation. V1's release-upon-acceptance timing statement disappears, although planned access for verified researchers remains.

R1.justification: The core literature comparison and creator-produced versus reader-inferred intent positioning remain. V3 omits the Radford et al. (2021) CLIP reference and adds limited positioning around broader MMD utility. NewsINT remains the same benchmark comparison despite its updated Wang citation.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the abstract and narrative, consistently emphasizes trustworthy news context, moves shortcut analyses into Section 4.3, and restructures Section 5 as Discussion. Limitations and ethics move into appendices; the existing appendices are reorganized, and an LLM usage statement is added. The author list also changes.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one, substantially reflowing tables, figures, and prompt boxes. Figure 1 uses a replacement example; Figures 2 and 4 are redesigned to foreground reference context; Figure 3's labels are reformatted. V3 adds the transfer-results table, style-example table, and fine-tuning prompt figure, while relocating several retained displays.

improvement.justification: V1 validates binary misleading labels but leaves realism and fidelity to the simulated desire and execution plan largely untested. V3 directly evaluates these central properties (Appendices E.2–E.3), substantially strengthening support for the benchmark's intent annotations. The documented external transfer experiment also supplies evidence of practical training utility. The unexplained removal of one desire-inference comparator reduces completeness, and single-run evaluation limits statistical assurance, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in benchmark validation and reproducibility.
